## Practical example: Two VLANs, one gateway owner
A controller is on VLAN 110 at 192.0.2.10/24; an AV device is on VLAN 120 at 198.51.100.20/24. Their gateways are 192.0.2.1 and 198.51.100.1, respectively.

**Cisco IOS XE 17.x router, isolated lab only:** Assume a supported GigabitEthernet0/0/0 interface and an already-up trunk carrying tagged VLANs 110/120. Verify interface names and feature support. These are documentation addresses, not production settings.

```text
configure terminal
ip routing
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0.110
 encapsulation dot1q 110
 ip address 192.0.2.1 255.255.255.0
 exit
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0.120
 encapsulation dot1q 120
 ip address 198.51.100.1 255.255.255.0
 exit
end
```

Each endpoint uses its own subnet's gateway. Do not also assign these gateway addresses to switch SVIs: pick the router OR the Layer 3 switch as gateway owner, not both.

This fragment enables routing without a security policy; it is not production-ready. No DHCP, Internet access, multicast routing or discovery relay is supplied. Test each gateway, then the actual AV application. Ping does not prove media/discovery works.

**Source:** [Cisco IOS XE 17.x: routing between VLANs with 802.1Q](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/td/docs/routers/ios/config/17-x/lan-wan/b-lan-wan/m_lnsw-conf-vlan-ieee.html). Example addresses and topology are BMT teaching choices.

## Practical example: Picture disappears, but the decoder still pings
Do not make “reboot everything” your first diagnostic tool. Record the failing source, receiver, VLAN and time, then compare that path with one that works:

1. **Physical path:** Check port errors, link speed and uplink utilization. A healthy ping is only a small unicast test.
2. **Membership:** Check whether the failing receiver's port appears in the switch's membership table for the stream's multicast group.
3. **Queries:** Verify a functioning active IGMP querier in that VLAN and that queries reach downstream switches. Snooping without working queries can let memberships expire.
4. **VLAN path:** Verify the correct VLAN crosses every inter-switch link in the path.
5. **Change one thing:** Compare membership before and after selecting the source again. Record whether the stream returns and whether the membership later disappears.

For Q-SYS, follow its version-specific networking guidance; do not assume a newer IGMP version automatically fixes an issue. Do not disable snooping across a live AV network as a casual experiment: flooding multicast may make things worse.

**Source:** [Q-SYS 10.1 multicast requirements](https://help.qsys.com/q-sys_10.1/content/Networking/Multicast_Traffic.htm). The checklist is a troubleshooting method, not proof that IGMP caused a particular fault.

## Practical example: A tiny SNMP test before building a dashboard
Start with a read-only question: “Can my monitoring laptop read the agent's uptime?”

**Net-SNMP 5.x client example:** In an isolated lab, the target is 192.0.2.20. An administrator has already configured a read-only SNMPv3 user named `av-read`, with `authPriv`, permitted OIDs and access limited to the monitoring host. Configure matching, supported authentication/privacy algorithms and credentials in the client's protected configuration, rather than putting passwords into a command that can land in shell history. Do not publish that configuration.

```sh
snmpget -v 3 -l authPriv -u av-read 192.0.2.20 .1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0
```

The numeric OID avoids needing a locally installed MIB just for this test. Run it twice: the returned uptime should advance. A reset can indicate an SNMP agent restart, not necessarily a whole-device reboot.

A timeout is not a diagnosis. Check address, reachability, UDP access, agent enablement, credentials and permitted source before changing settings. An authorization error can mean the user exists but cannot read that object. Do not use SNMP SET for this exercise.

**Sources:** [Net-SNMP GET tutorial](https://www.net-snmp.org/tutorial/tutorial-5/commands/snmpget.html), [SNMPv3 options](https://www.net-snmp.org/tutorial/tutorial-5/commands/snmpv3.html), and [client configuration protection](https://www.net-snmp.org/docs/man/snmp.conf.html).

## Practical example: Twelve powered devices do not equal “any 12-port PoE switch”
Suppose a lab design budgets four PoE+ devices at 30 W per switch port and eight PoE devices at 15.4 W per port:

- Four × 30 W = 120 W
- Eight × 15.4 W = 123.2 W
- Planned switch-side allocation = **243.2 W**
- An illustrative 25% design reserve adds 60.8 W, giving a **304 W target**.

That reserve is a planning choice, not an IEEE requirement. Check the real device classes, LLDP negotiation and switch allocation method; measured idle draw is not a safe substitute for required maximum allocation.

There are two separate checks: can each port supply the required PoE type, and can the installed power supplies support the total budget? A switch with enough ports can still fail either check. If redundant power matters, check the available PoE budget with one supply failed too.

PoE+ “30 W” is the switch-side figure; up to 25.5 W is available at the powered device under the standard's cable-loss allowance. Do not mix switch-side and device-side wattages in the same budget.

**Source:** [Cisco PoE power requirements reference](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/docs/wireless/catalyst-9100-access-points/215467-cisco-access-point-power-requirements-qu.html). The device counts and reserve are illustrative BMT arithmetic, not a product recommendation.

## Practical example: The laptop charges. Why is there no camera?
A USB-C plug tells you the connector shape, not the complete capability of the connection. A charging-capable cable can still be limited to USB 2.0 data. Higher charging wattage does not prove higher data speed or video support.

Before blaming the room system:

1. Check the laptop port's data, display and charging capabilities separately.
2. Check the cable's rated data speed, power rating and any required display support. Do not judge by the connector alone.
3. Check the dock or extender's upstream/downstream roles and supported USB speed.
4. Temporarily test with a short, known-good cable that meets the camera's documented requirements. Then reintroduce the longer path one piece at a time.

Some cameras work over USB 2.0, sometimes with different available modes. Others require USB 3.x for the intended format. Read the actual camera specification instead of assuming “USB-C means 4K.”

**Sources:** [USB-IF Type-C capability guidance](https://www.usb.org/sites/default/files/usb_type-c_language_product_and_packaging_guidelines_20230320.pdf) and [USB-IF cable markings](https://www.usb.org/cable_connector). The troubleshooting sequence is an illustrative commissioning method.

## NDI formats: choose the workflow, not a marketing label

**NDI High Bandwidth** uses the SpeedHQ codec. It is designed for high-quality, very-low-latency work on a capable LAN, at the cost of more network bandwidth. NDI's published format guidance gives approximate 1080p60 and 4K60 values of 130 Mb/s and 250 Mb/s respectively; real traffic varies with the sender, format and content. ([High Bandwidth format guide](https://docs.ndi.video/brand/ndi-formats/understanding-ndi-formats/ndi-high-bandwidth))

**NDI HX** is a family name for lower-bitrate workflows using H.264 or H.265/HEVC. You may encounter legacy **HX1**, then **HX2** and **HX3**. They are not interchangeable labels for the same stream. Current NDI guidance lists HX2 around 11–16 Mb/s at 1080p60 and HX3 around 50–62 Mb/s at 1080p60, depending on codec; it also publishes format-specific latency targets. Treat those as format/certification references—not guarantees for a particular camera, decoder, switch path, display, or production application. ([Format matrix](https://docs.ndi.video/all/using-ndi/ndi-for-video/ndi-video-codecs-and-format-matrix), [HX2](https://docs.ndi.video/brand/ndi-formats/understanding-ndi-formats/ndi-hx2), [HX3](https://docs.ndi.video/brand/ndi-formats/understanding-ndi-formats/ndi-hx3))

A useful shorthand is:

| Format | Typical trade-off | Check before specifying |
|---|---|---|
| High Bandwidth | More LAN bandwidth; high quality and low latency | NIC/uplink capacity and sender/receiver support |
| HX1 (legacy) | Older compressed workflow | Exact product and firmware compatibility |
| HX2 | Lower bitrate compressed workflow | H.264/HEVC support, decode resources and latency |
| HX3 | Compressed, lower-latency workflow | Exact codec, GOP/low-latency mode, sender/receiver support |

Do not assume an NDI receiver supports every NDI format a sender can produce. Verify the exact device firmware, application version and enabled license/features. OBS Studio requires a compatible third-party integration—DistroAV is the current successor to OBS-NDI—and its required OBS and NDI Runtime versions are maintained separately. vMix has its own version-specific NDI input/output settings. ([NDI's OBS guidance](https://docs.ndi.video/all/using-ndi/ndi-tools/plugins/obs), [vMix output documentation](https://www.vmix.com/help28/SettingsOutputs.html))

## Read the streaming diagram as two separate networks

The diagram above intentionally splits the workflow in two:

1. **Production LAN:** NDI cameras and an optional HDMI/SDI-to-NDI encoder feed a managed Gigabit switch. The production PC receives, switches and mixes these sources. An audio mixer or USB/network audio interface can feed the production PC directly or be embedded through a compatible source. Local confidence monitors or return feeds also consume LAN capacity.
2. **Internet contribution:** OBS or vMix encodes the finished program and sends it to the chosen platform using that platform's required ingest method—often RTMP/RTMPS, or SRT where the destination supports it. NDI itself is not a native public-platform stream protocol.

### Illustrative budget—not a universal design

Assume three 1080p60 High Bandwidth NDI cameras budgeted at 130 Mb/s each, one 30 Mb/s graphics source, and a production PC receiving all four:

```text
Camera/graphics input to production PC: (3 × 130) + 30 = 420 Mb/s
Finished platform stream upload:       8 Mb/s, for this example
```

The 8 Mb/s Internet upload is **not** added to the NDI camera traffic on the camera-switch uplink; it is a separately encoded output from the production PC. But the production PC's NIC, its switch port, and any uplink that aggregates source traffic still need room for all simultaneous NDI receives, monitor/return feeds, overhead and bursts. Increase the network budget for additional independent receivers or NDI program/preview outputs. Recording an already-received source can add disk/CPU load without another network copy; verify how the application actually receives and records it.

### Power and physical-network checks

- Verify each PoE camera's required standard/class and maximum power against both the switch-port capability and the total switch PoE budget.
- Prefer wired Ethernet for production NDI paths. Wi-Fi can be useful for deliberately tested, lower-bitrate contribution workflows, but changing RF conditions and retransmissions make it a poor default for primary cameras.
- Use full-duplex Gigabit Ethernet or faster where the measured aggregate requires it. NDI advises Gigabit as a baseline and calls out higher demands for High Bandwidth 4K and HX3 4K workflows. ([NDI switch guidance](https://docs.ndi.video/all/using-ndi/ndi-with-hardware/recommended-network-switch-settings-for-ndi))
- Measure the actual platform upload with a sustained test and leave operational headroom. An internet service's download speed says little about reliable outbound live-stream capacity.

## A practical first commissioning run

1. Connect one wired NDI camera and confirm format, frame rate and measured bitrate at the production PC.
2. Add each camera one at a time while monitoring switch-port utilization, errors and discards.
3. Add audio, confidence monitoring and recording in the combination used for the event.
4. Start the final platform encoder at the intended bitrate and test the actual outbound path.
5. Review end-to-end delay at the destination, not only the NDI source-to-PC view.

This method exposes aggregate NIC, switch, PoE and Internet limits before an audience does.
## Manufacturers: actual products, not blanket promises

NDI is supported across established camera and conversion manufacturers. These are examples of documented capabilities, not a shopping ranking or a claim that every product from the brand supports NDI. Verify the exact model, firmware, output mode and receiver before ordering.

| Manufacturer / example | Documented NDI capability | What this illustrates |
|---|---|---|
| [Panasonic AW-UE80](https://pro-av.panasonic.net/en/products/aw-ue80/spec.html) | High Bandwidth and HX2 included as standard; supported output modes differ | One camera can offer more than one NDI workflow. Check the NDI output-format table, not just the camera sensor resolution. |
| [Canon CR-N300](https://www.usa.canon.com/shop/p/cr-n300) | NDI HX2, with PoE+ connectivity | A PTZ can carry video, audio, control and power over one suitable Ethernet connection. |
| [Sony BRC-AM7](https://pro.sony/en_PR/products/ptz-cameras/ndi-hx-standard-support) | Sony lists NDI HX support without an additional license charge from release | License policy is model-specific. Other Sony models may require a firmware update or license activation. |
| [BirdDog X1 family](https://birddog.tv/x1/) | NDI HX3 | A current compressed-NDI camera family; check the individual model's resolution and output options. |
| [Magewell Pro Convert HDMI Plus](https://magewell.com/products/pro-convert-hdmi-plus) | Converts HD HDMI into NDI High Bandwidth, with loop-through | An existing HDMI camera or other compatible unprotected source can join an NDI system without being an NDI camera itself. |

An **encoder** creates an NDI source; a **decoder** turns a received source into an output such as HDMI. Some products do both, but do not assume that an encoder can also act as the overflow-room decoder. Likewise, a camera's available USB, HDMI, SDI and NDI modes may have different resolution limits or simultaneous-output restrictions.

## NDI carries audio too

NDI is not silent video with an audio cable bolted on afterward. A source can carry audio alongside its picture, and compatible software can send or receive audio-only sources. The application decides which channels it exposes, how they are mixed, and whether they follow video switching.

NDI supports several audio codecs; practical channel count depends on the codec and product. A stereo camera feed is not evidence that every NDI endpoint is stereo, nor does a protocol's multichannel capability guarantee that a particular application exposes all those channels. Confirm channel mapping, sample rate and routing in the actual transmitter and receiver. 48 kHz is a common live-production choice. ([NDI audio technical facts](https://docs.ndi.video/all/using-ndi/ndi-for-audio/technical-facts-about-ndi-for-audio))

### Keep the microphones from multiplying

For a simple streamed presentation, use one intentional program mix:

1. Microphones feed the mixer or DSP.
2. A USB audio interface, compatible network-audio input or camera embedding path brings that mix into the production computer.
3. Disable unused camera microphones and duplicate copies of the same mix.
4. Check left/right assignment and whether audio should remain constant or follow the selected camera.
5. Record a clap or slate, then adjust audio/video delay in the production software and listen to the finished recording.

A common mistake is accepting the same microphone through the mixer and two camera feeds. They arrive at different times, producing echo or comb filtering. More green meters do not mean better audio.

For remote guests, send a **mix-minus** return: the guest hears the host and program material, but not a delayed copy of their own voice. Keep local confidence-monitor speakers from feeding open microphones.

### NDI audio is not Dante or AES67

NDI does not internally use the same PTP-synchronized model as Dante/AES67. Its receiver can compensate for clock differences, but independent NDI endpoints should not be assumed to provide sample-aligned speaker outputs. NDI's own guidance distinguishes its latency and synchronization behavior from dedicated low-latency network-audio systems. ([NDI audio timing](https://docs.ndi.video/all/using-ndi/ndi-for-audio/technical-facts-about-ndi-for-audio))

Practical rule: NDI is useful for production feeds, recorded/streamed program audio and software workflows. Do not substitute it blindly for a stage-monitor, distributed loudspeaker or other tightly synchronized live-audio design. Measure the complete path, including application buffers and conversion.

A Dante microphone does **not** appear as an NDI audio source merely because both share a switch. A compatible interface, licensed software or explicit gateway must receive one protocol and produce the other. Document that bridge and test its channel mapping, latency and clock behavior. See [Lesson 20: Dante and AES67](/learn/it-for-av/dante-and-aes67).

## Free Windows tools you can actually use

[NDI Tools](https://ndi.video/tools/) is a free software collection. It does not make cameras, all NDI hardware upgrades, vMix licenses or third-party integrations free. Obtain the current installer from NDI, check its operating-system/GPU requirements, and review licenses before installing. Windows and Mac tool lists are different.

Start with a few tools rather than opening every application at once:

| Windows tool | Useful job |
|---|---|
| **Studio Monitor** | View and hear a source independently of the production application. A good first test when the camera is visible but OBS/vMix is unhappy. |
| **Test Patterns** | Generate a known test source so you can check the receiving path without a camera. |
| **Screen Capture** | Turn a presentation computer's desktop and selected audio into a network source. Close private windows and notifications first. |
| **Screen Capture HX** | A lower-bandwidth screen-capture option; verify supported GPU/encoder requirements. |
| **Webcam Input** | Present a selected NDI feed to compatible applications as a webcam-style input. Verify the receiving app's audio/video selections. |
| **Access Manager** | Configure discovery/group and network-source settings. Groups organize visibility, not security. |
| **Router** | Assign sources to named virtual outputs and recall routing presets. It is not a video mixer or an IP router. |
| **Bridge** | Connect deliberate remote NDI workflows across locations. This is not the same job as sending a finished show to a streaming platform. |

Sources and current platform list: [Windows tools](https://docs.ndi.video/all/using-ndi/ndi-tools/ndi-tools-for-windows), [Studio Monitor](https://docs.ndi.video/all/using-ndi/ndi-tools/ndi-tools-for-windows/studio-monitor), [Screen Capture](https://docs.ndi.video/all/using-ndi/ndi-tools/ndi-tools-for-windows/screen-capture), [Screen Capture HX](https://docs.ndi.video/all/using-ndi/ndi-tools/ndi-tools-for-windows/screen-capture-hx), [Webcam Input](https://docs.ndi.video/all/using-ndi/ndi-tools/ndi-tools-for-windows/webcam-input), [Router](https://docs.ndi.video/all/using-ndi/ndi-tools/ndi-tools-for-windows/router).

**Audio Direct** is a Windows-only collection of VST3 plug-ins for compatible audio applications. It can receive and generate multichannel NDI audio inside a supporting DAW. It is not automatically a system-wide replacement for every Windows audio driver. [Audio Direct documentation](https://docs.ndi.video/all/using-ndi/ndi-tools/plugins/audio-direct).

**NDI Free Audio** is a separate command-line utility for connecting an audio interface to NDI, with Windows, Linux and Mac workflows. Its available channels depend on the audio device; distribution/setup differs by platform. This is a useful next step for an audio-focused lab, not the first application a beginner needs to open. [Free Audio documentation](https://docs.ndi.video/all/developing-with-ndi/utilities/free-audio).

**NDI Analysis** is a diagnostic utility available separately from the Tools Launcher. Old tutorials may also recommend **NDI Remote**, which the current documentation labels discontinued. Use the current download/support pages rather than an old bundle from a random mirror. [Analysis](https://ndi.video/tools/analysis/), [Remote status](https://docs.ndi.video/all/using-ndi/ndi-tools/ndi-tools-for-windows/remote-discontinued).

### A free two-PC starter lab

1. On a trusted wired LAN, run Test Patterns or Screen Capture on PC A.
2. Open Studio Monitor on PC B and select that source.
3. Confirm picture and audio before adding production software.
4. Open a second receiver and observe how sender traffic changes.
5. If using OBS, install a compatible NDI integration such as DistroAV using its own current requirements; NDI Tools alone is not an OBS input plug-in.
6. Record locally and check lip sync before trying a public stream. Do not expose NDI services directly to the Internet to make discovery work.

## Where this setup earns its keep

These are illustrative workflows, not manufacturer-specific system designs.

### School studio or training room

Two PTZ cameras plus a teacher's Screen Capture feed enter the production PC. A USB mixer supplies the microphones. The operator switches camera/slides, records locally and sends one encoded program to the approved platform. Start with one receiver per source, then budget any additional preview stations.

### House of worship or small live event

Stage cameras and a graphics/presentation computer feed the production switcher. A dedicated broadcast mix arrives from the audio console; it need not be identical to the room's PA mix. Send a local NDI program output to a compatible decoder for an overflow display, and a separately encoded stream to online viewers. Check the overflow audio delay and disable unused camera microphones.

### Corporate town hall or hybrid meeting

Presenter cameras, slides and playback become production sources. A selected program feed can enter conferencing software through a compatible webcam-input workflow, while a separate stream/recording serves the broader audience. Remote presenters need a deliberate return video and mix-minus audio path; avoid routing the meeting's own received output back into its input.

### Why the room screen is not the public stream

An in-room confidence or overflow display usually needs a local output path. Pulling the public stream back from the Internet can add substantial platform delay. A direct HDMI/SDI output or a tested NDI decoder path is generally the more controllable choice; verify end-to-end delay for the actual application.
